topic: Matrix Multiplication as Composition of Linear Transformations
target_audience: Undergraduate students in Linear Algebra or Computer Graphics

outline.topic: Matrix Multiplication as Composition of Linear Transformations
outline.target_audience: Undergraduate students in Linear Algebra or Computer Graphics

sections.title: The Big Idea: Functions in Space
sections.content: Introduce the concept that a matrix isn't just a box of numbers, but a 'verb' that moves space. We visualize a 2D grid and a character (e.g., 'Leo the Lion') sitting on it. Explain that multiplying a vector by a matrix is like telling Leo where to move every point of his body simultaneously.
sections.example: Show Leo the Lion on a standard grid. Apply a 'Rotation' matrix to make him tilt 90 degrees. This introduces the matrix as a single transformation step.

sections.title: Prerequisite Check: The Basis Vectors
sections.content: Briefly recap that any linear transformation is defined entirely by what it does to the unit basis vectors i-hat (1,0) and j-hat (0,1). Visualizing these two arrows is the key to understanding the transformation matrix.
sections.example: Animate i-hat and j-hat landing on new coordinates (0,1) and (-1,0) respectively, forming the columns of a 90-degree rotation matrix.

sections.title: The Sequential Challenge: Two Steps, One Move
sections.content: Imagine Leo needs to rotate 90 degrees AND then stretch horizontally (shear). Traditionally, we would apply Matrix A, get a result, then apply Matrix B. Introduce the concept of 'Composition': finding a single 'Master Matrix' that does both in one leap.
sections.example: Visual: Leo rotates (Step 1), then the rotated Leo gets squashed horizontally (Step 2). The goal is to skip the middle step and go straight from the start to the squashed-rotated state.

sections.title: The Math: Why Right-to-Left?
sections.content: Explain the notation B(A(x)). Because the vector 'x' is on the right, the matrix closest to it (A) acts first. This explains why matrix multiplication order is written as B * A to mean 'A first, then B'. This is a critical point for student comprehension.
sections.example: Show the equation: Result = [Shear Matrix] * [Rotation Matrix] * [Leo's Vector]. Animate the matrices 'fusing' together into a single 2x2 matrix.

sections.title: Visual Derivation of the Product
sections.content: Show how to calculate the 'Master Matrix' by following the basis vectors through both transformations. We track where i-hat goes after Matrix A, then see where *that* new point goes under Matrix B. The final resting place of i-hat is the first column of the product matrix.
sections.example: Trace the path of i-hat: (1,0) -> Rotation -> (0,1) -> Shear -> (1,1). The first column of our new Master Matrix is now (1,1).

sections.title: Summary and Non-Commutativity
sections.content: Wrap up by emphasizing that Matrix Multiplication is simply functional composition. Use a final visual to show that order matters: rotating then shearing looks different than shearing then rotating.
sections.example: Split screen: Left side shows 'Rotate then Shear' Leo, Right side shows 'Shear then Rotate' Leo. They look completely different, proving AB is not equal to BA.

storyboard.title: The Big Idea: Functions in Space
lecture_lines: Matrices aren't just boxes; they are transformations.
Think of a matrix as a verb moving space.
Meet Leo the Lion on our coordinate grid.
This rotation matrix tilts Leo ninety degrees.
The entire space transforms as a single unit.
animations: Fade in a coordinate grid (#444444) and a simple character (Leo) at the origin.
The Leo character flashes #FFFF00 to draw attention.
A 2x2 matrix [[0, -1], [1, 0]] in #00FF00 appears at the top left.
The grid and Leo character rotate 90 degrees counter-clockwise.
The Leo character scales up slightly (1.2x) and back to emphasize its new position.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite Check: The Basis Vectors
lecture_lines: We track transformation using unit basis vectors.
Watch i-hat and j-hat land at new coordinates.
These new locations form the matrix columns.
animations: Display two arrows: i-hat (1,0) in #FF0000 and j-hat (0,1) in #00FF00.
Smoothly animate i-hat moving to (0,1) and j-hat moving to (-1,0).
Fade in a matrix where the first column is #FF0000 (0,1) and the second is #00FF00 (-1,0).

storyboard.title: The Sequential Challenge: Two Steps, One Move
lecture_lines: Suppose we rotate then shear our character.
Applying two separate matrices takes two steps.
We want a single Master Matrix instead.
This shortcut is called matrix composition.
It skips the middle step entirely.
animations: Show the Leo character on the standard grid.
Rotate the Leo 90 degrees CCW (Transformation A).
Shear the rotated Leo horizontally by factor 1 (Transformation B).
Fade out the intermediate state; show a new 'Master Matrix' C in #00FFFF.
Apply Matrix C to the original Leo, showing it move directly to the final sheared-rotated state.

storyboard.title: The Math: Why Right-to-Left?
lecture_lines: Matrix notation works from right to left.
The matrix closest to the vector acts first.
We combine these matrices into one single operation.
animations: Display the text 'B(A(x))' with A in #FFFF00 and B in #00FFFF.
Highlight 'A' and 'x' to show they are evaluated first.
Morph the symbols 'B * A' into a single symbol 'C' in #FFFFFF.

storyboard.title: Visual Derivation of the Product
lecture_lines: Track i-hat through the first rotation.
Next, apply the shear to its new position.
This final point becomes our first product column.
Follow j-hat to find the second column.
Now we have our composed transformation matrix.
animations: Display i-hat at (1,0) in #FF0000.
Animate i-hat moving to (0,1) using the first transformation.
Animate i-hat (at 0,1) moving to (1,1) using the second transformation.
Highlight the vector (1,1) as the first column of the result matrix.
Briefly show the same path for j-hat ending at its final position.

storyboard.title: Summary and Non-Commutativity
lecture_lines: Matrix multiplication is just combining functions.
Does the order of transformations change the result?
Rotating then shearing is not shearing then rotating.
animations: Split the screen into two halves, each with a Leo on a grid.
Left: Apply Rotation then Shear; Right: Apply Shear then Rotation.
Fade in a red 'not equal' sign (#FF0000) between the two resulting states.
